interactive.title: Two lines and a test point
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the squared grid from Straight-line graphs, running 0 to 8 across and 0 to 14 up. Line 1, solid, is y = 2x + 1. Line 2, dashed, is a second rule about the same x and y, and it has the two handles from y = mx + c. Its c handle slides its y-axis crossing up and down, and its m handle turns it about that crossing. A test point can be dragged anywhere, and it snaps to tenths. Under each rule a readout puts the point's x and y in, such as 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 ✓, and shows ≠ when the two sides differ, because a point is on a line only when the rule turns its x into its y. So a point fits both rules only where it is on both lines. A third readout gives the crossing, worked out from the two rules. At x = 0 the lines are c₂ − c₁ apart, and each 1 along the gap changes by m₁ − m₂, the difference of their tilts, so the gap shuts at x = (c₂ − c₁) ÷ (m₁ − m₂). As line 2's tilt nears line 1's while their c's differ, the gap changes more slowly and the crossing runs off the grid. When the tilts match, the gap never changes, the lines are parallel and the readout says no crossing. When the c's match too, line 2 lies on top of line 1 and the readout says same line. On the screen about readings, the grid zooms in round the crossing with tenths marked. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows rules or lines and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? puts the pairs into both rules.
interactive.ignores: The test point snaps to tenths so the sums stay readable, but x and y can be any numbers, including ones like 4/3 that no tenth hits exactly. The grid shows a short piece of each line, which carries on both ways, so a crossing off the grid is still a crossing. Lines straight up, such as x = 3, have no m, so the tilt test here does not cover them. The rules and the call-out prices are example values.

explain.text:
Two facts like x + y = 7 about the same two unknown numbers each draw a straight line, and the pair of numbers that fits both facts is the point where the lines cross.[^1] Start with one fact, y = 2x + 1. Pick any x, work out its y, and you have a pair that fits, such as (0, 1), (1, 3) or (2, 5), and so does every point on the line between them. One equation in two unknowns has endless answers,[^2] and plotted they make the rule's line, as in Straight-line graphs. Drag the test point onto line 1 and its readout ticks. Move it off and the readout shows ≠, because a point off the line has a y the rule does not give for its x.

Now add a second fact about the same x and y, x + y = 7, drawn as the dashed line 2. Its own answers fill its own line, such as (0, 7), (3, 4) and (7, 0). You want the pair that makes both equations true at once.[^3] A point fits a rule only when it is on that rule's line, so a pair that fits both must be on both lines, and two lines that cross share just one point, the crossing. There the x is the same on both lines, and so is the y. Two equations solved together like this are [[simultaneous equations]], simultaneous meaning true at the same time, and a pair that fits them both is a [[solution]]. Here line 1 starts 6 below line 2 at x = 0 and climbs 3 more for each 1 along, so the gap shrinks by 3 a step and shuts once, at x = 2. So there is one solution, the [[crossing point]] (2, 5): 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 and 2 + 5 = 7. Solving each equation alone does not find it. (3, 7) fits y = 2x + 1, but 3 + 7 = 10, not 7, so it is on line 1 and misses line 2.

Turn line 2 and the crossing point moves. Written as y = −x + 7, line 2 has m = −1 against line 1's 2. Turn it to y = 1.5x + 7. At x = 0 it is 6 above line 1, and each 1 along line 1 climbs 0.5 more than line 2, so the gap shuts by 0.5 a step and closes at x = 12, off the grid. The solution is still there, and the grid just does not show it. Turn line 2 to the same tilt, y = 2x + 7, and the gap stays 6 all the way along, so the lines are parallel, never cross, and there is no solution.[^1] Slide its c down to 1 as well and line 2 lies on top of line 1, so every pair on it fits both, and there are endless solutions.[^4] So for two lines written as y = mx + c, read m and c before you draw. Different m's give one crossing point, because the gap changes by the same amount for each 1 along and so passes zero once. The same m with different c's gives none. The same m and the same c give one line.

A graph gives a reading, which is not always exact. y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 5 cross between the tenths, and the nearest the test point gets, (1.3, 3.7), fits x + y = 5 but gives 2 × 1.3 + 1 = 3.6, not 3.7. So put a reading back into both equations, and if it is a little out, it is an estimate. Worked out from the gap, 4 ÷ 3, the crossing is at x = 4/3 exactly, and the next two lessons turn that sum into a method for any pair of equations. The marine electro-technology syllabus has you solve circuit problems with Kirchhoff's laws by simultaneous equations in two unknowns.[^5] The course's two-battery puzzle is one of these: two equations in the two unknown currents, and the currents the batteries give are the pair that fits both, where their lines cross. **The pair of numbers that makes two equations true at once is the point where their lines cross;[^1] parallel lines give no solution,[^1] and the same line gives endless solutions.[^4]**

analogy.text: Two firms quote for the same job. One charges a £60 call-out and £30 an hour, the other a £20 call-out and £50 an hour. Each firm's bill against hours is a line, with the call-out as c and the hourly rate as m. They charge the same only where the lines cross, at 2 hours and £120, as 60 + 30 × 2 = 120 and 20 + 50 × 2 = 120. Two firms with the same hourly rate and different call-outs never charge the same, and two identical price lists charge the same for every job.
analogy.breaks: A job's hours are never below zero, and a firm may bill in whole or part hours, so a real bill climbs in steps and the matching bill may fall between two of them. The lines in the lesson carry on both ways and through every fraction.

practice.text:
- Write each equation as y = mx + c, doing the same to both sides.
- Read the two m's and c's first. Different m's give one crossing point. The same m with different c's gives parallel lines and no solution. The same m and c give the same line and endless solutions.
- Draw each line through three points its rule gives. Make the grid wide enough to hold the crossing, as close m's can put it far away.
- Read the crossing point, then put it into both equations. If both come out true, it is the solution. If one is a little out, your reading is an estimate.
- A line straight up, such as x = 3, has no m, so the m and c test does not cover it. It still crosses any line that is not straight up, once.

**Rule of thumb:** A pair that fits one equation is on one line. Only a pair that fits both is a solution.

**Worked example:** y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8. The second is y = −x + 8, so the m's are 2 and −1. They differ, so there is one crossing point. Line 1 passes (0, −1), (2, 3) and (4, 7). Line 2 passes (0, 8), (4, 4) and (8, 0). They cross at (3, 5). Check: 2 × 3 − 1 = 5 and 3 + 5 = 8, both true, so x = 3 and y = 5.

**Common mistakes**
- Solving one equation alone. (4, 7) fits y = 2x − 1, but 4 + 7 = 11, not 8.
- Expecting every pair of equations to have an answer. Parallel lines, such as y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x − 4, have none.
- Taking no crossing on the grid to mean no answer. y = 2x + 1 and y = 1.8x + 7 cross at x = 30.
- Taking a reading as exact. Put it back into both equations. If one is a little out, it is an estimate.
- Guessing pairs until both fit. It is slow, and whole-number guesses miss a crossing that is not a whole number: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 5 cross at x = 4/3, which no whole number or tenth hits.
- Missing that two rules are the same line written differently, such as y = 2x + 1 and 2y = 4x + 2. Every point on it fits both.

interactive.html:
A squared grid, 0 to 8 across and 0 to 14 up, with two straight lines and a test point. Every rule here is an example.

A faint ring marks what you can drag. The test point snaps to tenths, c to whole numbers, m to tenths.
interactive.title: Two lines and a test point
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a point making both rules tick only where the two lines meet, and that crossing running off the grid as the tilts draw level, when you drag the point and turn line 2.

checks.label: If the two lines cross, the coordinates of this intersection are the solutions to the simultaneous equations, and if the lines are parallel there is no solution: wherever a ring marks the crossing both rules give it the same y, a scan of every tenth finds only the crossing fitting both, the test point lights there and not on one line alone, and lines with the same m and different c show no crossing

Equations that have more than one unknown can have an infinite number of solutions: every tenth along each line drawn fits its own rule, between and beyond the whole numbers, and the first puzzle takes endless pairs as its answer

When the two equations were really the same line, there were infinitely many solutions: halved, the rule on the same-line screen is line one's own rule and is drawn exactly on top of it, every tenth along it fits both rules, the crossing readout says same line, and the puzzle's rule that rearranges to line one is its answer

We are looking for the ordered pairs that make both equations true: each puzzle's right pair fits both rules, every wrong pair offered misses at least one, and a wrong pair shows a ≠ under the rule it misses and no halo

Every worked row is right, by hand: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, and 7 ≠ 5; 3 + 7 = 10; (2, 5) from 6 ÷ 3; (6, 13) at m = 1; (12, 25) from 6 ÷ 0.5; (30, 61) from 6 ÷ 0.2; a gap that stays 6; 2 × 7 = 14 = 4 × 3 + 2; (1, 3); 3.6 and 4.9 near 4 ÷ 3 = 4/3; 2.4, not 2.2; (3, 9) from 9 ÷ 3; and the call-out bills meet at 2 hours and £120

As line 2's tilt nears line 1's the crossing runs off the grid: with c = 7, m = −1, 1, 1.5, 1.8 and 1.9 put it at x = 2, 6, 12, 30 and 60, ringed on the grid only for the first two and pointed to by an arrow beyond, as is x = −12 at m = 2.5; m = 2 gives no crossing, and m = 2 with c = 1 the same line

A reading from the graph is an estimate: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 5 cross at x = 4 ÷ 3, which no tenth hits, so no tenth in the zoomed grid fits both rules; the test point dropped on the crossing lands on (1.3, 3.7), which fits line 2 but gives 3.6 on line 1

Dragging: the test point snaps to tenths inside the grid and clings to a line or the crossing it is dropped near; the c handle slides along the y-axis in whole numbers and moves only c; the m handle, 1 along, turns line 2 in tenths and moves only m

Before an answer a puzzle keeps back what it asks and its readouts read ?; a right answer or Why? draws it and fills them in; every answer offered is checked against the puzzle's own rules, and every wrong one has a hint of its own
Every demonstration finishes arriving within its 3 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; a puzzle's drawing after an answer or Why? finishes within 2.5 s

warnings: SVG labels "0.4" and "0.5" are only 4 px apart on one row, so they read as one: leave at least 4 px between them, or label only what differs (at step = step 12, and 1 more setting) [at 340 px wide]

applied: practice.text: 'doing the same to every term' is wrong for adding or taking away (x + y = 7 minus x from every term gives y − x = 7 − x); also 'close m's put it far away' fails when the c's are close too, and guessing only fails for whole-number guesses.

explain.text: 'Two facts about the same two unknown numbers each draw a straight line' is untrue in general (xy = 12 draws a curve); only facts of the x + y = 7 kind draw straight lines, so the opening needs scoping.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt: When line 2's c equals line 1's, the lines cross at x = 0 whatever the tilts, so the crossing does not run off the grid; and if line 2 is steeper with a higher c the gap grows rather than shuts.
